links.note: 81 says all of staying at home and guarding one's goods (இருந்தோம்பி இல்வாழ்வதெல்லாம்) is for tending guests and doing them good; 212 says all the wealth produced by effort (தாளாற்றித் தந்த பொருளெல்லாம்) is for doing good to the deserving. Both end on the identical line வேளாண்மை செய்தற் பொருட்டு, so the household and earned wealth are given the same single purpose in two chapters.

81 makes the guest the purpose of the whole household life (இல்வாழ்வதெல்லாம் ... விருந்தோம்பி). 43 lists the guest (விருந்து) as one of five the householder must tend, alongside ancestors, gods, kin and oneself (ஐம்புலத்தாறு ஓம்பல் தலை). Read together, 81's 'all' is the hospitality chapter's emphasis on one duty that 43 sets among five.

82 says eating alone while the guest is outside (விருந்து புறத்ததாத் தானுண்டல்) is not to be desired even if the food were the medicine against death. 229 says eating by oneself alone (தாமே தமியர் உணல்) to fill up one's store is more bitter than begging. Both judge the solitary meal itself, one by setting it against the best imaginable food and the other against the worst condition.

82 uses the deathless medicine (சாவா மருந்து, which Parimelazhagar glosses as அமிழ்தம்) as the best food there could be, and says even that should not be eaten with the guest shut out. 64 says gruel stirred by one's children's small hands is far sweeter than அமிழ்து. In both the nectar is the benchmark that a human tie outranks: the food's worth depends on who is at the meal.

83 says the life of one who tends the arriving guest every day (வைகலும் ஓம்புவான்) does not suffer and go to ruin (பருவந்து பாழ்படுதல் இன்று). 227 says the disease called hunger rarely touches one accustomed to sharing his food (பாத்தூண் மரீஇயவனை). Both promise that habitual sharing of food protects the sharer from want, once for the host of guests and once for the giver to the poor.

83 says daily hospitality never brings a household to ruin (பாழ்படுதல் இன்று), which Parimelazhagar takes to mean the host's goods are not used up. 480 says helpfulness that does not weigh the extent of what one has (உளவரை தூக்காத ஒப்புரவாண்மை) quickly ends one's wealth (வல்லைக் கெடும்). The Book of Wealth thus attaches a condition of measure to the kind of promise 83 makes without one.

In 84 the fair goddess (செய்யாள்) dwells with a glad heart in the house of one who tends guests with a glad face. In 167 the same goddess (செய்யவள்) cannot bear the envious man and shows him to her elder sister (தவ்வையைக் காட்டி விடும்). Fortune is pictured as a person who stays or leaves according to how the householder regards other people: welcome keeps her, envy sends her away.

84 has the goddess of fortune (செய்யாள்) living in the home of the glad-faced host. 617 says she of the lotus (தாமரையினாள்) lives in the effort of the unslothful (மடியிலான் தாளுளாள்), and her dark sister in sloth. The same figure is given two different dwellings, generosity in the Book of Virtue and exertion in the Book of Wealth.

84 pairs அகனமர்ந்து (with a glad heart, said of the goddess) with முகனமர்ந்து (with a glad face, said of the host). 92 reuses the same two words: sweet speech with a glad face (முகனமர்ந்து இன்சொலன்) is better than giving with a glad heart (அகனமர்ந்து ஈதல்). The repeated formula ties the hospitality chapter to the next one, and in both it is the visible face that the verse singles out.

85 asks whether one who feeds guests and eats what is left (விருந்தோம்பி மிச்சில் மிசைவான்) need even sow his field (வித்தும் இடல்வேண்டும் கொல்லோ); Parimelazhagar supplies that it will bear by itself. 1039 says that if the owner stays away and does not go to it (செல்லான் கிழவன் இருப்பின்), the land sulks like a wife. The conflict holds only if 85 is taken literally, as Parimelazhagar does, and not as a figure of praise; Kalaignar reads 85 quite differently, as asking whether such a host would hold back even his seed-grain.

85 implies that the field of the host who feeds guests first yields without sowing. 545 says rain and harvest gather together (பெயலும் விளையுளும் தொக்கு) in the land of the king who wields the sceptre as he should. In both, right conduct is said to make the land fruitful, at the scale of one household's field and at the scale of a kingdom.

86 says one who tends the departing guest and watches for the next (வருவிருந்து பார்த்திருப்பான்) will be a good guest to those in the sky (வானத்தவர்க்கு). 50 says one who lives on earth as one should (வாழ்வாங்கு வாழ்பவன்) will be placed among the gods who dwell in the sky (வான்உறையும் தெய்வத்துள்). 86 names one specific practice that earns what 50 promises the householder in general, and turns it into a reciprocity: the host becomes the guest. (This edition prints நல்வருந்து in 86 and உநற்யும் in 50; both are typos.)

87 says the fruit of the sacrifice of hospitality has no fixed measure and is as great as the guest (விருந்தின் துணைத்துணை), which Parimelazhagar takes as the guest's worth. 105 says help is not bounded by the help itself but by the worth of those it was done for (செயப்பட்டார் சால்பின் வரைத்து); Parimelazhagar reads 105 as being about help given in return. The same rule of measuring an act by its recipient and not its size appears in hospitality and in gratitude.

On Parimelazhagar's reading, 87 scales the fruit of hospitality to the guest's worth (விருந்தின் துணைத்துணை). 221 says giving to those who have nothing (வறியார்க்கு ஒன்று ஈவதே ஈகை) is the only real giving, and all the rest is like a loan expecting return. One verse values the gift by the receiver's merit and the other by the receiver's need; the conflict depends on reading துணை in 87 as merit and on treating feeding a guest and giving as the same kind of act.

87 calls hospitality a வேள்வி (sacrifice) whose fruit has no fixed measure; Parimelazhagar notes it is one of the five great sacrifices. 259 says not taking a life and eating it is better than pouring oblations in a thousand sacrifices (அவிசொரிந்து ஆயிரம் வேட்டலின்). In both verses the ritual word is used to rank an ethical practice: one is named a sacrifice, the other is set above a thousand of them.

88 says those who do not take up the sacrifice of tending guests guard their goods painfully (பரிந்தோம்பி) and end by saying 'we have no support' (பற்றற்றேம்). 228 asks whether the hard-eyed who store what they have and lose it (வைத்திழக்கும்) do not know the joy of giving. Both describe the same sequence of hoarding and then loss, and both set it against a use of wealth the hoarder never tried.

88 pictures people guarding their goods with pain (பரிந்தோம்பி) and still losing them. 376 says what is not allotted to one will not stay even if guarded with pain (பரியினும் ஆகாவாம் பாலல்ல), and what is one's own will not leave even if poured away (சொரியினும் போகா தம). The fate chapter gives a general ground for 88's observation: anxious guarding does not decide whether wealth stays, so spending it on guests risks nothing that guarding would have saved.

89 calls the folly that neglects hospitality 'poverty within having' (உடைமையுள் இன்மை) and says it is found among fools (மடவார்கண்). 153 calls turning away a guest 'the poverty of poverties' (இன்மையுள் இன்மை விருந்தொரால்) and then names bearing with fools (மடவார்ப் பொறை) the strength of strengths. The forbearance chapter reuses both the formula and the word மடவார், with inhospitality as its standard example of the worst lack. (This edition misprints the first word of 153.)

89 says poverty in the midst of wealth is the folly (மடமை) of not caring for guests. 841 says lack of understanding is the poverty of poverties (அறிவின்மை இன்மையுள் இன்மை) and that the world does not count other lack as lack. 841 states as a general principle what 89 shows in one case: the real want is a failure of understanding, whatever one owns.

89 says the inhospitable fool is poor while possessing (உடைமையுள் இன்மை). 1005 says those who neither give nor enjoy have nothing even with crores piled up (அடுக்கிய கோடி உண்டாயினும் இல்). Both verses, in the Book of Virtue and the Book of Wealth, deny that unused wealth counts as having.

90 says the anicham flower wilts when merely smelled (மோப்பக் குழையும் அனிச்சம்) and a guest wilts at a look from a changed face. In 1111 the man addresses the anicham, grants its delicate nature (நன்னீரை) and says the woman he loves is more delicate still (நின்னினும் மென்னீரள்). The flower is the book's standard of fragility in both places; 90 applies it to a guest's feelings and the lover to a woman's person, each claiming something more delicate than the flower.

90 says a guest wilts when looked at with an altered face (முகந்திரிந்து நோக்க). 707 says nothing is as knowing as the face, since whether one is pleased or angry it gets there first (உவப்பினும் காயினும் தான்முந்துறும்). 707 explains why 90's guest is hurt before a word is spoken: the face has already reported the host's mind.

90 gives the negative case: a face that turns (முகந்திரிந்து) and looks makes the guest wilt. 93 gives the positive rule in nearly the same terms: with a glad face, looking sweetly (முகத்தான் அமர்ந்து இனிது நோக்கி), then sweet words from the heart. The last verse of the hospitality chapter and the third of the next share the face-and-look sequence; Parimelazhagar on 90 also lists the glad face, the sweet word and the good deed as successive stages of welcome.

91 defines sweet words (இன்சொல்) as words mixed with tenderness and free of deceit (ஈரம் அளைஇப் படிறு இலவாம்). 911 says the இன்சொல் of women who want a man's wealth and not out of love (அன்பின் விழையார் பொருள்விழையும்) will bring him harm (இழுக்குத் தரும்). 911 uses the same word for speech that fails both of 91's tests, which shows the definition in 91 is doing real work: pleasant sound without love is not what chapter 10 praises.

91 says sweet words are the speech of those who have seen the செம்பொருள் (செம்பொருள் கண்டார் வாய்ச்சொல்), which Parimelazhagar glosses here as those who know virtue. 358 defines understanding as seeing the செம்பொருள் so that the folly of birth departs (செம்பொருள் காண்பது அறிவு). The same phrase links ordinary kind speech to the insight the renunciation chapters describe, though the commentator gives the word a more modest sense in 91.

92 says being sweet-spoken with a glad face is better than giving with a glad heart (அகன்அமர்ந்து ஈதலின் நன்றே). 295 says one who speaks truth in accord with his heart (மனத்தொடு வாய்மை மொழியின்) is above those who do austerity together with giving (தவத்தொடு தானஞ்செய்வாரின் தலை). Twice the book ranks a quality of speech above material giving, once for kindness and once for truthfulness.

92 ranks sweet speech with a glad face above glad-hearted giving. 387 says the world answers to the word of one able to give with sweet words and protect (இன்சொலால் ஈத்தளிக்க வல்லார்க்கு); 525 likewise joins கொடுத்தலும் இன்சொலும். Where the Book of Wealth describes what actually wins people, the two are combined and not ranked, so 92's comparison reads as a statement about relative worth, not advice to speak kindly in place of giving.

93 says virtue lies in sweet words that come from within (அகத்தானாம் இன்சொலினதே அறம்), after a glad face and a kind look. 34 says being spotless in mind is the whole of virtue and the rest is noisy show (ஆகுல நீர பிற); Parimelazhagar counts speech and outward guise among that rest. 93's word அகத்தானாம் is what keeps sweet speech on the right side of 34's line: it counts as virtue because it issues from the mind.

93 requires the glad face and the sweet word to come from within (முகத்தான் அமர்ந்து ... அகத்தானாம்). 786 says friendship that makes only the face smile is not friendship; friendship that makes the heart within smile is (முகநக ... நெஞ்சத்து அகநக). The same முகம்/அகம் pairing sets the test of genuineness for kind speech and for friendship.

93 places virtue in a glad face followed by sweet words from within (அகத்தானாம்). 824 warns that deceivers who smile sweetly with the face and are bitter within (முகத்தின் இனிய நகாஅ அகத்தின்னா வஞ்சரை) are to be feared. 824 describes the counterfeit of 93's first half, so the outward signs 93 begins with cannot by themselves be taken as proof of the inner part.

94 says want that brings suffering (துன்புறூஉம் துவ்வாமை) does not come to those whose sweet speech gives joy to everyone. 566 says that if a ruler is harsh of speech and without kindly regard (கடுஞ்சொல்லன் கண்ணிலன்), his long-standing wealth perishes on the spot. The two verses state the same link between speech and prosperity from opposite sides, for anyone in the Book of Virtue and for a king in the Book of Wealth.

94 asserts that sweet speakers do not fall into want, without saying how. 525 says one who can give and speak sweetly (கொடுத்தலும் இன்சொலும் ஆற்றின்) will be surrounded by layer on layer of kin (அடுக்கிய சுற்றத்தால் சுற்றப்படும்). 525 supplies a worldly mechanism for 94's promise: sweet speech gathers people around one, and a person so surrounded is not left destitute.

95 says being humble and sweet-spoken (பணிவுடையன் இன்சொலன் ஆதல்) is a person's ornament and nothing else is. 125 says bowing (பணிதல்) is good for everyone and for the rich it is a further wealth (செல்வர்க்கே செல்வம் தகைத்து). Both treat humility as an added possession, an ornament in one verse and wealth in the other, and 125 says who gains most from it.

95 makes humility (பணிவு) the true ornament (அணி). 978 says greatness always bows (பணியுமாம்) while smallness adorns itself in self-admiration (அணியுமாம் தன்னை வியந்து). The same two roots are set against each other in 978: the small person's self-adornment is the false ornament, and the bowing 95 praises is what the great actually wear.

95 says humility and sweet speech are a person's ornament and other things are not (அணியல்ல மற்றுப் பிற). 1014 asks whether shame is not the ornament of the worthy (அணிஅன்றோ நாணுடைமை சான்றோர்க்கு), and 575 names kindly regard as the eye's ornament. The exclusive wording of 95 is therefore the chapter's emphasis: other chapters award the same title to other inner qualities, while agreeing with 95 (as Parimelazhagar reads it) that bodily ornaments are not meant.

96 says that if one seeks out good things and says them sweetly (நல்லவை நாடி இனிய சொலின்), what is not virtue wears away and virtue grows. 128 says that if even one harmful word has its effect (ஒன்றானும் தீச்சொல் பொருட்பயன் உண்டாயின்), what was good turns out not good. Together they give speech power over one's stock of virtue in both directions: good words build it and a single bad word undoes it.

35 defines virtue as what proceeds without slipping into four things, the last being painful speech (இன்னாச்சொல்). 96 says virtue grows and its opposite wears away when one speaks good things sweetly (அல்லவை தேய அறம்பெருகும்). 35 only requires avoiding harsh words; 96 adds that the positive practice of sweet, well-chosen speech actively increases virtue.

97 says speech that yields benefit and does not part from pleasantness (பயன்ஈன்று பண்பின் தலைப்பிரியாச் சொல்) produces நயன் and brings forth good (நன்றி). 194 says speech with no benefit and no pleasantness (பயன்சாராப் பண்பில்சொல்) is without நயன் and removes one from good (நன்மையின் நீக்கும்). The four terms பயன், பண்பு, நயன் and நன்மை recur in the negative, so 194 is 97 inverted; Parimelazhagar glosses பண்பு as sweetness and நயன் as justice in both.

97 asks for speech that has both benefit (பயன்) and pleasantness (பண்பு), and credits it with producing நயன். 197 says the worthy may say what lacks நயன் if they must, but should not say what lacks பயன் (நயனில சொல்லினும் சொல்லுக ... பயனில சொல்லாமை நன்று). 197 thus ranks the qualities 97 holds together: use is the one that cannot be given up. Parimelazhagar takes நயன் in 197 as justice; Subramuniyaswami takes it as pleasantness, which makes the limit on chapter 10 more direct.

98 says sweet speech that is clear of smallness (சிறுமையுள் நீங்கிய இன்சொல்) gives joy in the next life and this one; Parimelazhagar explains சிறுமை as causing pain to others by what the words mean. 291 defines truth as speech containing no harm at all (யாதொன்றும் தீமை இலாத சொலல்). Sweetness and truthfulness are both defined by the same test, the absence of harm to others, and not by sound or by literal accuracy. (This edition prints சிறுமையுவு in 98, a typo for சிறுமையுள்.)

98 says sweet speech free of smallness gives joy (இன்சொல் ... இன்பம் தரும்) here and hereafter. 911 says the sweet speech of women who desire wealth and not the man brings harm (இன்சொல் இழுக்குத் தரும்). The two predicates answer each other, and the condition in 98 (சிறுமையுள் நீங்கிய) marks the difference: what 98 promises holds only for sweet words that are not serving a mean purpose.

99 asks why one who sees how sweetly sweet words yield (இன்சொல் இனிதீன்றல் காண்பான்) would use harsh words (எவன்கொலோ வன்சொல் வழங்குவது); Parimelazhagar takes it as one who has felt the pleasure of others' kind words to himself. 318 asks why one who knows what is painful to his own life does painful things to other lives (என்கொலோ மன்னுயிர்க்கு இன்னா செயல்). The two rhetorical questions have the same form and the same argument from one's own experience to the treatment of others, applied to words in 99 and to harm in general in 318. (The first line of 318 is misprinted in this edition, but the verse is recoverable.)

99 asks what could lead someone who knows the good that sweet words do to use harsh ones (வன்சொல்). 784 says friendship is not for laughing together but for going ahead to rebuke when a friend oversteps (மிகுதிக்கண் மேற்சென்று இடித்தற் பொருட்டு). The friendship chapter supplies a case where sharp words have a purpose, so 99's question is best read as aimed at needless harshness and not at every hard word.

100 says speaking unpleasant things when pleasant ones are available is like taking the unripe fruit when the ripe is there (கனிஇருப்பக் காய்கவர்ந்தற்று). 1306, a speech in the Book of Love, says that love without serious and light quarrels is like over-ripe fruit and unripe fruit (கனியும் கருக்காயும் அற்று). The ripe/unripe pair is used differently: in 100 the ripe fruit is simply the right choice, while the lover treats fruit that is too ripe and fruit that is too raw as two ways of missing the right point.

100 pictures someone who has ripe fruit at hand and takes the unripe: unpleasant words chosen while pleasant ones exist (இனிய உளவாக இன்னாத கூறல்). 831 defines folly as taking hold of harm and letting gain go (ஏதங்கொண்டு ஊதியம் போக விடல்). Harsh speech in 100 is an instance of exactly the choice 831 names as folly, which fits the chapter's closing argument that harsh words are a bad bargain for the speaker as well as wrong.
